papers.title: Floral scent diversity and evolution in deceptive Cypripedium, and post-pollination effects on floral scent and its biosynthesis in C. henryi
papers.abstract: Background and Aims: Floral scent is a primary driver of pollinator attraction and reproductive isolation in deceptive orchids. Yet, little is known about the variation and evolution of scent in a phylogenetic framework and how pollination affects the biosynthesis and emission of scents in these lineages. This study characterizes scent diversity across Cypripedium, a genus of deceptive orchids, examines phylogenetic constraints, and investigates post-pollination effects on scent composition in one of the species. Methods: Floral volatile organic compounds (VOCs) were sampled from 31 Cypripedium taxa using dynamic headspace techniques, and analysed by gas chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry (GC/MS). Uni- and multivariate methods were used to analyse intra- and interspecific scent variation and test for phylogenetic signal in floral scent. Post-pollination effects on scent composition were experimentally tested in C. henryi using four pollination treatments, combined with RNA-seq analyses of floral tissues to examine transcriptional responses in VOC biosynthetic pathways. Key results: We detected 258 floral VOCs, revealing a high chemical diversity dominated by terpenoids, aliphatics, and aromatic compounds. Floral scent composition was highly species-specific, and closely related taxa often shared only few compounds. Scent composition differed among pollination groups, but these groups explained only a limited proportion of overall scent variation. We detected a significant but weak phylogenetic signal, suggesting limited evolutionary constraint in floral scent. Pollination had limited effect on C. henryis floral scent and volatile biosynthesis gene expression, despite a significant decrease in total scent emission after pollinium deposition. Transcriptional changes predominantly occurred in the petals rather than the labellum and staminode. Conclusion: Floral scent evolution in Cypripedium is characterized by high chemical diversity, and a weak phylogenetic constraint, consistent with variable selection in food-deceptive systems. The pollination study further suggests the absence of a strong, directed post-pollination effect on the floral scent of C. henryi. Keywords: Cypripedium; deceptive pollination; floral scent; volatile organic compounds (VOCs); phylogenetic signal; linalool; post-pollination effects; transcriptome profiles; differential gene expression; floral organs

papers.title: Temporal genomic imprinting regulates grain filling in barley
papers.abstract: In cereals, the persistent endosperm accumulates starch and storage proteins, making their grains a major source of food and feed. Early grain development is epigenetically controlled through the parent-of-origin-specific expression of imprinted genes in the endosperm that regulate endosperm proliferation, nutrient accumulation and embryo nourishment. Imprinted genes have been identified in several major cereals, and a few have been functionally characterized. However, it is unclear how imprinted genes regulate the accumulation of storage compounds in cereal grains. Through spatiotemporal transcriptome analysis of 255 imprinted genes in barley (Hordeum vulgare), we identify endosperm transfer cells in grains as a hotspot of expression of imprinted genes. Furthermore, we show that transcription factor LYS3 dynamically regulates grain filling in barley through early expression of the maternal allele, followed by partial activation of the paternal allele.

papers.title: Steering Before Selection: Energy-Limited Developmental Control as a Phenotypic Capacitor, a Pre-Specified Simulation Study
papers.abstract: Living systems meet environmental change at several speeds: fast physiological control during development, slower learned memory, and genetic change through selection. We asked whether developmental control, which we interpret as bioelectric and which carries a continuous energy cost, steers evolution, and we report what survived twenty-two versions of individual-based simulation, pre-specified from version 11 onwards. After a permanent environmental change, sensing absorbed the change within about 25 generations and genes took over through selection alone 340 to 450 generations later in every seed, a result replicated in a fresh pre-specified test on 20 new seeds. Control did not guide genetic change; it concealed genetic variation from selection. Control hid three to six times more harmful load than no control, and an energy shortfall released it; brief release outperformed prolonged release, and release helped only when control re-locked around the new form. The net value of release depended mainly on whether the concealed harmful load was kept in check: without reversal of harmful mutations it was a cost at 500 individuals (mean fitness 0.103 against 0.122 without control), whereas with reversal it was a benefit at every population size from 250 to 4,000 (0.632 against 0.489 at 2,000). A test that separated the factors showed that population size alone did not reverse the result and that the cost lay in the concealment itself, with release recovering part of it. We conclude that energy-funded developmental control buys time while selection rewrites the genes, conceals rather than directs variation, and acts as an energy-switched phenotypic capacitor whose value depends mainly on whether the harmful load it conceals is kept in check. The models are abstract and contain no voltages or channels, so the bioelectric reading is an interpretation and all results are model results. We set out predictions for testing these claims in developing embryos.

papers.title: Replication-coupled maturation of readthrough late transcripts by a polyomavirus small T antigen
papers.abstract: Productive polyomavirus gene expression requires the maturation of long, non-polyadenylated "wraparound" transcripts generated by late-strand readthrough of the polyadenylation signal on the circular genome, giving rise to structural protein mRNAs and microRNAs. In Merkel cell polyomavirus (MCV), small T (sT) antigen, along with large T (LT) antigen-mediated DNA replication, drives this process. Deletion of sT (MCV{Delta}sT) attenuates late gene transcription, abolishes splicing, eliminates VP1 expression, and traps unspliced transcripts in the nucleus. Exogenous sT restored transcription and splicing in an aphidicolin-sensitive manner, requiring domains that activate DNA replication and bind chromatin. RNA sequencing revealed that sT promotes splicing and polyadenylation of wraparound transcripts, thereby increasing cytoplasmic VP1 and VP2 mRNA levels. A dual-fluorescence reporter confirmed that the leaky late poly(A) signal (LpA) was used more efficiently upon sT expression, indicating enhanced polyadenylation. Co-expression with LT abolished this effect, likely by overwhelming the capacity of the polyadenylation machinery. sT from HPyV7 and HPyV9 could similarly rescue this defect, indicating that this regulatory activity is conserved in a subset of sT proteins. Together, these findings define sT as a replication-coupled regulator of late transcript expression, splicing, and polyadenylation, revealing how a compact DNA virus converts readthrough transcription into productive gene expression.

papers.title: RubisCO-encoding methanotrophs elicit a coordinated transcriptional response to carbon dioxide limitation.
papers.abstract: The methanotroph Methylococcus capsulatus encodes the carbon dioxide (CO2)-fixing enzyme ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (RubisCO), which, along with CO2 and methane (CH4), are required for growth of this bacterium. This unique, dual one-carbon metabolism is present in phylogenetically diverse methanotrophs and is likely widespread in nature, but the connection between organic and inorganic carbon metabolism in these methanotrophs is unclear. Here we used a systems approach to investigate the requisite role of CO2 in M. capsulatus metabolism and physiology. We show that atmospheric CO2 levels are sufficient for M. capsulatus cultivation, and that CO2 assimilation is linked to cellular redox balance. In the absence of CO2, M. capsulatus elicits a global transcriptional response that includes induction of RubisCO- and other inorganic carbon assimilation-encoding genes with a concomitant decrease in ribosome biogenesis and nitrogen assimilation genes typical of a bacterial stringent response. This CO2 starvation response balances biosynthesis with carbon availability. Genetic and biochemical evidence show that a LysR-type transcriptional regulator (CbbR) activates RubisCO and other CO2 assimilation gene transcription via direct promoter binding in response to elevated intracellular RubisCO substrate, ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate, in CO2-starved cells. These results offer insights into the essentiality of CO2 for M. capsulatus metabolism and establish a function for CbbR-family regulators in methanotrophs beyond their canonical association with CO2 fixation in autotrophic bacteria.

papers.title: A new Serratia taxon found in a trombidiform mite shows genomic evidence of host adaptation but is phylogenetically distinct from Serratia symbiotica
papers.abstract: Abstract The evolutionary transition from free-living bacteria to host-adapted symbionts is typically accompanied by substantial genomic changes. Within the genus Serratia, this transition has so far been documented only in the aphid-associated species, Serratia symbiotica, whereas all other Serratia species are free-living. In this study, we identify a putatively new Serratia taxon using metagenomic approaches in the trombidiform mite, Halotydeus destructor. We provide genomic evidence for a possible transition to a host-adapted lifestyle in this new Serratia sp., which sits phylogenetically within a clade of free-living Serratia species. The genomic signatures of evolving toward a host-adapted lifestyle include a reduced genome size and coding capacity, an elevated transposase fraction, and detectable chromosomal rearrangements, relative to other free-living Serratia species. However, the species does not show the same structure of genome reduction as S. symbiotica. Functional gene content analyses including COG categories and virulence factor repertoires also showed that our new Serratia sp. had a distinct gene profile from both free-living Serratia and S. symbiotica. Additional genomic screening suggests that infections of the new Serratia sp. are common in wild populations of H. destructor across its invasive Australian range, warranting future investigations on the possible role this symbiont plays in the evolutionary ecology of its mite host. Our work not only highlights a potential parallel transition to a host-adapted lifestyle in the Serratia genus, but also represents the first characterisation of a possible host-adapted Serratia taxon in a trombidiform mite.

papers.title: Evolutionary and acclimatory shifts in ion transporter gene expression across salinity transitions in the copepod Eurytemora carolleeae
papers.abstract: Many aquatic invaders are crossing biogeographic boundaries from saline to freshwater habitats. This transition often requires acclimation or evolution of physiological mechanisms to maintain internal ionic homeostasis. Populations of the copepod Eurytemora affinis complex have repeatedly invaded freshwater environments from saline habitats over the past century, providing an ideal model for investigating rapid adaptation to salinity change. Prior studies have found that ion transport-related genes form the largest functional categories of genes under selection and show evolutionary shifts in gene expression across saline to freshwater transitions in the E. affinis complex. In this study, focusing on the top targets of selection, we investigated evolutionary and acclimatory shifts in gene expression for 19 ion transport-related genes for populations of E. carolleeae (Atlantic clade of the E. affinis complex). Using a quantitative real-time PCR approach, we compared gene expression between ancestral saline and derived freshwater populations through a common garden reaction norm experiment and a laboratory natural selection experiment. We found that different ion transport-related gene paralogs within expanded gene families showed divergent patterns of expression in response to salinity change, consistent with specialization. For instance, Na+/K+-ATPase subunit paralog 1 (NKA--1) and Na+,K+,2Cl- cotransporter paralog 3 (NKCC-3) exhibited the evolution of increased expression in the freshwater population across all conditions, relative to the saline population. In contrast, Na+/H+ antiporter paralog 7 (NHA-7) and NHA-5 showed evolution of elevated expression in the saline population under low salinity relative to the freshwater population. Several genes also showed evolutionary differences in plasticity between saline and freshwater populations, such that saline populations retained phenotypic plasticity, whereas freshwater populations were comparatively canalized. In the laboratory natural selection experiment imposing salinity decline, evolutionary responses of the paralogs NKCC-3, NHA-5, and NHA-7 in the saline selection line largely recapitulated the evolutionary shifts observed in the natural populations. On the other hand, expression patterns of the ion transporters in the freshwater selection line showed little response during salinity increase, suggesting canalization. Together, these results reveal evolutionary and acclimatory divergence in gene expression among paralogs, suggesting the evolution of functional divergence among them.

papers.title: SedaDNA metabarcoding reveals hidden histories of within-species sequence variation
papers.abstract: Most genetic data come from contemporary populations, leaving historical changes in within-species variation poorly documented. Sedimentary ancient DNA (sedaDNA) offers an opportunity to recover historical sequence variation, but its potential to reconstruct temporal changes in within-species composition remains underexplored. Here, we analysed dated sediment cores from eight Atlantic and Mediterranean coastal wetlands using COI and 18S metabarcoding, treating amplicon sequence variants as putative haplotypes. Across native, non-indigenous and cryptogenic taxa, accumulated haplotype diversity and geographic sharing varied markedly among species and markers, without consistently distinguishing species status. Temporal reconstructions revealed that accumulated haplotype networks combined distinct sets of variants detected across historical periods. Broader analyses of 18S data further showed substantial variation in haplotype composition among periods, sites and taxa. By resolving the temporal and spatial distributions of within-species sequence variants, our findings demonstrate how sedimentary DNA archives can uncover historical dimensions of biodiversity obscured by time-aggregated analyses, establishing a foundation for historical metaphylogeography.

papers.title: RBM25 selectively stabilizes XBP1s mRNA independently of splicing factor activity
papers.abstract: The unfolded protein response (UPR) preserves endoplasmic reticulum (ER) proteostasis through coordinated transcriptional and translational programs that promote adaptation and prevents apoptosis. A central component of this response is the IRE1-XBP1 signaling axis, in which IRE1-mediated unconventional splicing of XBP1 mRNA generates the active transcription factor XBP1s. While the mechanisms governing IRE1 activation and XBP1 splicing have been extensively characterized, the post-transcriptional processes that sustain XBP1s expression remain poorly understood. Here, we identify RNA-binding motif protein 25 (RBM25) as a key post-transcriptional regulator of the UPR that selectively stabilizes spliced XBP1 mRNA during ER stress. RBM25 binds the XBP1s 3' untranslated region and prolongs XBP1s mRNA half-life without affecting unspliced XBP1u transcripts or IRE1-dependent regulated decay (RIDD) targets. Consequently, RBM25 depletion diminishes XBP1 transcriptional output, compromises adaptive UPR signaling, and sensitizes cells to ER stress-induced death across multiple stress paradigms. Together, our findings uncover a previously unrecognized RNA-based regulatory checkpoint that amplifies and sustains XBP1 signaling, thereby tuning the magnitude of the adaptive UPR and cellular survival under proteotoxic stress.

papers.title: Phage-Inducible Chromosomal Jumbo Islands (PICJIs) spreading antimicrobial resistance, host-adaptation factors and defense systems, a novel satellite family of nucleus-forming Chimalliviridae
papers.abstract: Phage satellites are mobile genetic elements that depend on helper bacteriophages to promote their own dissemination. Here, we identified a novel family of large satellites, named Phage-Inducible Chromosomal Jumbo Islands (PICJIs), that are widespread in Escherichia coli and Salmonella enterica among diverse hosts, worldwide. These largest satellites to date (71.6 {+/-} 15.8 kbp) are specifically transduced by the persistent jumbo bacteriophage Goslarvirus of the nucleus-forming Chimalliviridae family. Furthermore, PICJIs carried numerous accessory genes associated with clinically relevant antimicrobial resistances, host-adaptation, and several anti-phage defense systems.

papers.title: Functional genomic characterization of anti-phage defense systems in vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium
papers.abstract: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) is a significant public health threat, demonstrating high rates of antibiotic resistance and frequently causing hospital-acquired infections. Bacteriophages (phages) are a promising adjunctive therapy to reduce bacterial load and manage VREfm infections. Many bacteria encode anti-phage defense systems--groups of genes that can counteract phage infection--but these systems have not been characterized in VREfm. Here we explored the diversity of anti-phage defense systems within clinical VREfm isolate genomes and examined their impact on phage susceptibility. We first used two available bioinformatic tools (DefenseFinder and PADLOC) to identify putative anti-phage defense systems in 21 hybrid-assembled VREfm clinical isolate genomes, and observed that most anti-phage defense systems were located on plasmids, defense islands, and prophages. Combining this information with functional testing of phage susceptibility did not reveal robust associations between specific defense systems and resistance to four VREfm-targeting lytic phages. Due to inherent limitations of phage susceptibility testing, we next developed an assay to assess phage survival after co-incubation with bacteria, and identified over two dozen genes associated with phage killing, including a potentially novel defense island. Lastly, we attempted to functionally validate 10 candidate anti-phage defense systems, only four of which were ultimately tested in enterococci. Expression of one of these candidates, AbiE, decreased bacterial susceptibility to two Enterococcus-targeting phages. As VREfm-targeting phage therapy becomes more widely available, identification of genes contributing to phage resistance can aid in streamlining the provision of phages to patients who could benefit from this new therapeutic modality.

papers.title: Functional analysis of small-molecule and protein binding domains using monomeric streptavidin-based two-component biosensors
papers.abstract: Protein biosensors are important analytical and diagnostic tools that convert molecular recognition into measurable activity. Most common two-component biosensors require two non-competing recognition domains, yet binding affinity and specificity alone do not reliably predict their compatibility with the rest of the biosensor. We report a modular platform that exploits monomeric streptavidin (mSA2) as a surrogate recognition domain, enabling rapid functional evaluation of candidate binders in the context of biosensor scaffold without requiring a second ligand-specific binding protein. We established a chromatography-free protocol for recovering functional mSA2-based biosensor components from Escherichia coli. Using biotinylated small molecules methotrexate and vitamin D3, as well as heart failure protein biomarkers galectin-3 and S100A7 we demonstrate ligand-dependent reporter biosensor activation. The developed platform provides a scalable approach for rapid binder evaluation and biosensor prototyping, streamlining biosensor development using binding domains generated by directed evolution or computational protein design.

papers.title: Sex-specific growth in invasive pink salmon (Oncorhynchus gorbuscha) from two regions in northern Norway
papers.abstract: The recent invasion of pink salmon (Oncorhynchus gorbuscha) along the Norwegian coast has raised significant ecological concerns. Investigating regional differences in marine growth is an important step in evaluating the establishment of pink salmon in new environments. Pink salmon were captured in two northern Norwegian fjords during their return migration to in the summer of 2023; Varangerfjord in Finnmark and Oksfjord in Troms, representing the eastern and western extent of the core areas of the pink salmon invasion. Body size estimates (total length, weight, condition factor) were used to identify differences in sex-specific marine growth at the time of capture. Scales were analyzed to estimate marine somatic growth via the distance between circuli and the position of the last winter circuli (LWC). Estimates of cumulative circuli distance were divided into four marine growth periods that roughly correspond to 1) spring/summer, year one, 2) summer/fall, year one, 3) fall/winter, year one, and 4) spring, year two. Sex-specific and location effects were found in the body size of pink salmon, where males were heavier and had higher body condition than females and Varanger males had the highest estimates of body size. Scale readings revealed that growth rates were highest in the spring of both years (periods 1 and 4), with significantly decreased growth in the fall/winter (periods 2 and 3). Males from the established Varanger location exhibited the highest growth (17-21% total cumulative circuli distance) over all periods compared to the other groups, suggesting that these fish experience more favorable survivorship and marine growth conditions. These insights into pink salmon marine growth emphasize the importance of taking sex and location into consideration in further assessing the species' expansive potential in Norway.

papers.title: Phenotypic plasticity segregates antagonistic species but undermines their coexistence
papers.abstract: Environmental change often induces novel phenotypes in multiple cohabiting species, yet how such common-cue-induced plasticity shapes their coexistence is largely unknown. Testing this link requires disentangling inducing-environment effects from induced-phenotype effects, which remains elusive. We address this gap using two mutually antagonistic bacterial species, Staphylococcus aureus (Sa) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa). In habitual salinity, where both bacteria show unicellularity, Pa severely diminished Sa. In contrast, high salinity induced macroscopic cell clustering that spatially segregated Sa and Pa (Sa: bottom-dwelling vertical filament; Pa: top-dwelling horizontal mat), and led to >10-fold higher coexistence than habitual salinity. Counterintuitively, physically inhibiting cell clustering (abolishing segregation) in high salinity led to a further >100-fold higher coexistence (Sa:Pa::~1:1). This was because salinity-induced clustering was adaptive for Pa, but not for Sa: such adaptive plasticity enabled killer Pa to proliferate by monopolizing oxygen, which diminished Sa in a correlated manner, thereby weakening coexistence (mechanistically explained by diffusion-based killing). Hence, although the inducing environment promoted overall coexistence, the induced phenotype undermined it. Community-wide genomics revealed that the high level of coexistence achieved by abolishing segregation in high salinity allowed rapid coculture-specific evolution. Taken together, we uncover how plasticity can appear to promote antagonistic coexistence despite causally undermining it.

papers.title: Platelet-endothelial crosstalk drives distinct endothelial dysfunction in bicuspid aortic valve disease
papers.abstract: Background: Bicuspid aortic valves (BAV) predispose individuals to premature development of aortic stenosis (AS). The abnormal hemodynamic environment of BAV affects both platelets and valvular endothelial cells (VECs), but whether platelet-derived signals contribute to valve morphology-specific endothelial dysfunction remains unknown. Methods: Platelets and VECs were obtained from patients with BAVs or tricuspid aortic valves (TAVs) undergoing valve replacement for AS. Platelets were activated to generate platelet releasate (PR). PR composition and its effects on VECs were investigated using complementary molecular, multi-omic, functional, and computational approaches. Results: BAV and TAV patients exhibited markedly distinct PR profiles, which translated into differential endothelial responses. Strikingly, BAV-derived PR elicited a substantially more pronounced endothelial dysfunction phenotype, characterized by widespread molecular reprogramming and functional alterations. Integrated multi-omics uncovered mitochondrial dysfunction as a central feature of BAV PR-induced endothelial injury, accompanied by activation of pathways spanning endothelial remodeling, migration, and immune-cell recruitment. These molecular signatures translated into mitochondrial depolarization, altered mitochondrial dynamics, enhanced VEC migration, and increased neutrophil adhesion and chemotaxis. Finally, computational ligand-receptor and ligand-target analyses identified candidate signaling axes linking platelet-derived mediators to endothelial reprogramming, highlighting potential therapeutic targets. Conclusions: We provide the first direct evidence that platelet activation contributes to AS initiation through the induction of endothelial dysfunction and that these effects are amplified in BAV. These findings identify platelet-VEC crosstalk as a previously unrecognized mechanism linking abnormal valve hemodynamics to disease onset. Targeting platelet-derived mediators may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for AS, specifically in BAV.

papers.title: The YjfJ protein is the effector of a second PspA/VIPP1 system that is widespread in the Gammaproteobacteria
papers.abstract: Maintaining the integrity of the cytoplasmic membrane is essential for bacterial cell survival. Unsurprisingly, prokaryotes have evolved conserved mechanisms by which they sense, maintain, and repair membrane integrity in response to stress. The phage shock protein (Psp) is one such system, understood primarily through work undertaken in the Gammaproteobacterial species Escherichia coli and Yersinia enterocolitica. The system utilises an effector, PspA, alongside accessory proteins that sense stress and recruit PspA to damaged membranes. Homologues of PspA - part of the PspA/VIPP1 family - are found in a variety of bacterial phyla. Although most work in the Gammaproteobacteria has concerned the canonical Psp response, there have been descriptions of non-canonical PspA/VIPP1-containing systems that warrant further genomic analysis. By analysing the PspA/VIPP1 content of a diverse selection of Gammaproteobacterial genomes, we reveal the existence of two phylogenetically distinct subtypes of PspA/VIPP1 proteins, PspA- and YjfJ-like, which are found at similar frequencies. The YjfJ-like proteins are not only a novel subtype of PspA/VIPP1, having their own unique set of accessory proteins, but in some species, such as the ESKAPE pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa, comprise the only PspA/VIPP1-containing system. Our study positions the YjfJ-like containing systems on equal footing with the PspA system in terms of their conservation and distribution in the Gammaproteobacteria. This suggests that studies into the biological functions of YjfJ-like proteins would be well-justified from their unique presence in some important human pathogens.

papers.title: Lung Epithelial TLR7 is a Factor in Viral Replication and Pathogenesis
papers.abstract: Respiratory virus infections are the leading causes of morbidity and mortality of infants and the elderly worldwide. Currently it is not known how Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) vaccination of infants can cause enhancement of RSV disease, highlighting gaps in our understanding about how viruses like RSV interact with the immune system. Here we address this and show that ERK MAP kinase signaling from Toll-like Receptor-7 (TLR7) detection of RSV and influenza, but not human parainfluenza virus type 3 (HPIV3), infections in bronchial epithelial cells (BECs) drives replication of the viruses. Virus infection is detected by pattern recognition receptors like TLR7 that bind to single stranded RNA (ssRNA) viral replication intermediates in late endosomes. Here we report that TLR7 is expressed in BECs and detects RSV ssRNA, causing ERK MAP kinase signaling. RSV and influenza use this detection and signaling in BECs to drive its replication and infection, a mechanism that counters TLR7s role in antiviral defence. Experimental blockade of TLR7 binding or downstream signalling through ERK MAP kinase decreased RSV and influenza replication, but had no effect on HPIV3. RSV viral loads in mouse and human females were higher compared to males, consistent with higher sex-dependent expression of the TLR7 gene from two copies of the X chromosome in females. In a TLR7 gain of function mouse model there was a significant enhancement of RSV replication and RSV eosinophilic and Th2 disease markers like interleukin-5 (IL-5). In summary, TLR7 is expressed in human lung BECs in the lungs where it acts as a factor in RSV and influenza replication and disease pathogenesis. We propose that this is a major factor in determining the sex-disparity of viral disease.

papers.title: Sarrella massiliensis gen. nov. sp. nov., a new gut genus isolated from the stool of a healthy donor
papers.abstract: Strain Marseille-QA0792 (=CSUR QA0792, CECT 31199) was isolated from the feces of a healthy person using the culturomics method. The fecal sample originated from leftover material collected for a fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) procedure, obtained during a routine screening in accordance with the guidelines of the French National Agency for Medicines and Health Products Safety (ANSM). This strain is Gram-stain-negative, rod-shaped, non-motile, and non-spore-forming. It is strictly anaerobic, with optimal growth at 37{degrees}C. Strain Marseille-QA0792 presented its highest 16S rRNA identity, 96.2%, with ''Merdibacter massiliensis'' strain Marseille-P3254 (not validly published) (accession number LT598590) and ANI similarity of 75.0% with the same species. Among validly published species, strain Marseille-QA0792 showed its highest 16S rRNA gene sequence similarity (91.5%) with Faecalicoccus acidiformans strain 37-2a (accession number HQ452864), whereas all computed average nucleotide identity (ANI) values were below 75%. Genome sequencing revealed a genome size of 2.67 Mb and a G+C content of 50.01%. This species is classified within the Erysipelotrichaceae family in the Bacillota phylum. Thus, we isolated for the first time a novel genus named Sarrella massiliensis gen. nov., sp. nov., strain Marseille-QA0792. This discovery highlights the importance of continuing culturomics efforts to explore the human microbiome.

papers.title: Intestinal molecular siphoning by engineered bacterial spores for non-systemic treatment of nicotine addiction
papers.abstract: Eradicating toxic small molecules from the body typically requires the administrations of therapeutic agents for systemic circulation and tissue distribution, resulting in inevitable adverse events from off-target effects. Here, we propose a intestinal molecular siphoning approach for treating diseases caused by toxic substances, in which enzymatic degradation of a toxic substance in the intestinal lumen serves as a driving force for the diffusion of the toxic substance from blood to gut, and continuous elimination of the toxic substance in the gut could effectively ease substance dependence. Using nicotine as a model substance, a live bacterial system was constructed by displaying a trypsin-resistant nicotine oxidase on the surface of Bacillus subtilis spores, and encapsulating in enteric-coated microspheres for gastric protection and targeted intestinal release. After oral treatments with the live bacterial system in mice, peak concentrations of nicotine in blood and brain were remarkably reduced compared to controls. Moreover, the live bacterial system could effectively attenuate nicotine addiction by suppressing dopamine reward surges to reverse withdrawal hyperalgesia, preventing the upregulation of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, and alleviating anxiety-like behaviors. These findings show the potential of intestinal molecular siphoning as a target-independent therapeutic strategy for lowering circulating toxic substances through non-systemic enzyme reprogramming.

papers.title: Photographic age gap is associated with frailty and predicts survival in laboratory mice
papers.abstract: Ageing studies in mice need biomarkers that are cheap, non-invasive and repeatable. We asked how much of a mouse's age can be read from an ordinary photograph, and whether the part that cannot be explained by age carries biological information. We assembled 2,846 photographs of 1,292 mice (four strains, 1 to 34 months old) from seven facilities and predicted age with a frozen self-supervised vision model (DINOv2) and a ridge regression, always tested on facilities the model had never seen. Absolute age transferred poorly between facilities (median absolute error 138 days), because each facility's photographs carried an offset. Relative age transferred well: among mice photographed in the same session, the older mouse was predicted older in 65% of pairs, rising above 95% for age differences over 500 days, and the later photograph of the same mouse was predicted older in 63% of repeat pairs. Sex, in comparison, was inferred more reliably (87%). Mice predicted older than their age were frailer (+0.12 SD per 100 days) and had shorter survival (hazard ratio 1.14 per 100 days), and fourth generation (G4) telomerase-deficient mice looked 151 days older than their wild-type controls. Routine photographs therefore carry a real biological age signal that can be read at no extra cost, best used to compare mice photographed together.

papers.title: The bHLH121-CAT2 module maintains root tip redox homeostasis to confer salt tolerance additively with the SOS pathway in Arabidopsis
papers.abstract: Soil salinity inhibits plant growth, in part, by restricting the availability of essential mineral nutrients such as iron (Fe). Although Fe deficiency frequently coincides with salt stress in the field, the molecular mechanisms integrating Fe homeostasis with salt tolerance remain largely unknown. Here, we identify the Fe deficiency response regulator bHLH121 as a key coordinator of salt tolerance in Arabidopsis. Loss-of-function mutants of bHLH121 exhibit pronounced hypersensitivity to salt stress, with severely impaired primary root elongation and reduced seedling biomass. Transcriptomic and histochemical analyses reveal that bHLH121 is required to maintain reactive oxygen species (ROS) homeostasis specifically in root tips under salt stress. We further demonstrate that CATALASE 2 (CAT2) is a direct downstream target of bHLH121, and that CAT2 overexpression fully rescues the salt hypersensitivity of the bhlh121 mutant. Importantly, this bHLH121-CAT2 module operates independently of the classical SOS pathway, as sos2 bhlh121 double mutants display additive salt sensitivity. Together, our findings uncover a novel regulatory module in which bHLH121 governs root tip redox homeostasis through CAT2 to confer salt tolerance, providing a direct mechanistic link between the Fe regulatory network and abiotic stress resilience in plants.

papers.title: Pervasive chromothripsis drives pleural mesothelioma to impact gene function and patient survival
papers.abstract: Pleural mesothelioma (PM) is a tumour type showing high structural complexity but the full spectrum of variants present and their impacts are poorly understood. We comprehensively describe the mutational landscape of mesothelioma, exploiting a large (N=443) cohort profiling the tumour genome and transcriptome in parallel. We find that the majority of candidate driver variants are mediated by copy number alterations (CNAs) and discover high frequencies of complex rearrangements across most tumours, dominated by chromothripsis (74% of tumours) and chromoplexy (59%). Chromothripsis contributes to significant CNA hotspots to delete known PM tumour suppressor genes such as CDKN2A, NF2 and BAP1, thought to be among the earliest events in PM development; and the presence of chromothripsis is associated with significantly worse patient survival. We also discover multi-faceted crosstalk between the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes during PM evolution, involving alterations to both genomes, and mitochondrial expression changes associated with subtypes and chromothripsis.

papers.title: Life on leaves left a lasting mark on the Methylobacterium core genome
papers.abstract: The extent to which core genomes reflect strictly vertical inheritance remains debated, particularly in ecologically diverse bacterial lineages. Here, we investigate the evolution of the core genome of Methylobacterium, a major leaf-associated bacterial genus, to assess how evolutionary signals vary across genes and whether they relate to functions involved in adaptation to life at the surface of plant leaves (the phyllosphere). Identifying 1,099 protein-coding core genes across 293 genomes, we combined gene tree comparisons, phylogenetic network reconstruction, nucleotide polymorphism patterns, and functional enrichment analyses. We found that most core genes show some deviation from the consensus phylogenetic tree. However, this discordance is not randomly distributed. Across all analytical approaches, genes showing the strongest deviations are consistently associated with functions linked to life in the phyllosphere, including anoxygenic photosynthesis, protection against UV and osmotic stress. These genes are often grouped into conserved clusters in the genome. In particular, a large cluster involved in anoxygenic photosynthesis, including bacteriochlorophyll and carotenoid biosynthesis, shows strong variation in its evolutionary history and organization across lineages, despite maintaining a conserved core structure. Similar patterns of phylogenetic incongruence and gene organization are observed across related Hyphomicrobiales inhabiting the phyllosphere, suggesting that these functions extend beyond Methylobacterium. Together, these results indicate that evolutionary heterogeneity within the core genome is concentrated in genes involved in key ecological functions. While alternative explanations cannot be excluded, these patterns are consistent with horizontal gene transfer contributing to the diversification of traits important for survival and adaptation in phyllosphere bacterial communities.

papers.title: MoALE1, an ART-like effector, contributes to rice blast virulence through host immune suppression
papers.abstract: Rice blast, caused by the hemibiotrophic fungus Magnaporthe oryzae, is one of the most destructive diseases affecting rice production worldwide. During infection, M. oryzae secretes effector proteins that suppress host immunity and facilitate colonization. Here, we characterized MoALE1, a predicted effector that is structurally similar to members of the heat-labile enterotoxin/cholera toxin family. Using a yeast secretion trap assay, we demonstrated that MoALE1 contains a functional signal peptide. A MoALE1-GFP fusion localized to the biotrophic interfacial complex, indicating that MoALE1 is a cytoplasmic effector. Expression analyses revealed that MoALE1 is expressed during biotrophy, from 16 to 48 h post-inoculation. Transient expression in Nicotiana benthamiana showed that MoALE1 suppresses BAX-mediated cell death, suggesting a role in host immune suppression. To investigate its contribution to pathogenicity, a{Delta} moale1 mutant was generated and evaluated in rice infection assays. Deletion of MoALE1 significantly reduced disease severity but did not affect fungal growth, stress tolerance, sporulation, appressorium development, host penetration, or early invasive growth. In contrast, infection by the {Delta}moale1 mutant resulted in enhanced host H2O2 accumulation and increased expression of ROS-associated defense genes. Together, these findings identify MoALE1 as a biotrophy-associated cytoplasmic effector that promotes rice blast pathogenicity by suppressing host immune responses and provide new insight into the function of ADP-ribosyltransferase (ART)-like effector candidates in M. oryzae .

papers.title: Phosphate-responsive ornithine lipid biosynthesis remodels outer membrane composition and contributes to polymyxin tolerance
papers.abstract: Bacteria frequently encounter environments in which essential nutrients are limiting. Phosphate limitation constrains phospholipid synthesis and challenges maintenance of the cell envelope. While many Gram-negative bacteria respond by producing phosphorous-free membrane lipids, the mechanisms and consequences of this remodeling remain poorly understood in Enterobacterales. Here, we characterize the genetic and physiological basis of ornithine lipid (OL) biosynthesis in the opportunistic pathogens Enterobacter cloacae and Klebsiella pneumoniae. We show that OL biosynthesis depends on OlsF, a bifunctional acyltransferase that catalyzes both acylation steps required for OL synthesis. Phosphate limitation promotes OlsF-dependent OL accumulation through the PhoBR two-component system. Membrane fractionation revealed that OlsF-derived OLs are present in both membrane compartments but are enriched in the outer membrane. OlsF-dependent OL production enhances polymyxin tolerance during phosphate limitation, linking nutrient availability to changes in antimicrobial susceptibility. Together, these findings identify OlsF-dependent OL synthesis as a phosphate-responsive membrane remodeling pathway that reshapes outer membrane composition and influences the physiological properties of the Gram-negative cell envelope.

papers.title: Antibiotic-induced protein mislocalization drives hypervesiculation in Salmonella
papers.abstract: The incorporation of cytosolic proteins into bacterial outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) has remained mechanistically unresolved, as these proteins are normally excluded from vesiculation sites by the inner membrane (IM) barrier. Here, we show that antibiotic-induced envelope perturbation compromises this spatial barrier, enabling an aberrant interaction between proteins that are ordinarily segregated across cellular compartments and thereby promoting MV formation in Salmonella. Exposure to non-lethal cephalexin (LEX) induced robust hypervesiculation, accompanied by inhibition of the essential division penicillin binding protein (PBP) 3 and accumulation of the PBP5. Under envelope perturbing conditions, PBP5 accumulated at lateral sites associated with MV emergence and promoted periplasmic crowding independently of its catalytic activity. A cytosolic acyl carrier protein (ACP) emerged as a PBP5 interacting partner under LEX exposure, coinciding with cryogenic electron microscopy detected IM perturbation and aberrant ACP mislocalization. Formation of the PBP5 ACP complex promoted PBP5 accumulation, resulting in periplasmic crowding, progressive weakening of outer membrane peptidoglycan tethering, and ultimately MV formation. Together, these findings uncover a mechanism whereby stress-induced disruption of subcellular compartmentalization enables a non-canonical interaction between normally segregated proteins, driving hypervesiculation in Salmonella.

papers.title: High-throughput, single-cell-encoded colony imaging reveals infection-linked heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Phenotypic heterogeneity within bacterial populations shapes adaptation, antibiotic tolerance, and infection dynamics, yet colony-level quantification remains difficult at scale and on dark/selective media. We present HeteroTyper, an automated, high-throughput time-lapse platform that measures colony phenotypes across >100 plates per run on both transparent and dark media. HeteroTyper includes a ready-to-use computational pipeline that can be deployed on common plate-imaging setups and across agar types, delivering appearance times as a proxy for lag times, growth trajectories, colony size, intensity, and morphology from routine image series. Automated counts closely matched manual counts, supporting accuracy and scalability. Using Yersinia pseudotuberculosis as a model, HeteroTyper resolves phenotypic heterogeneity in vitro, with early and late phases showing broader appearance time distributions than mid-log phases. It also reveals organ-specific heterogeneity in vivo, with mesenteric lymph node isolates displaying the broadest appearance time distributions compared to spleen and liver. Appearance time was negatively associated with final colony size and intensity, linking growth initiation to downstream colony outcomes. Together, these distribution-level measurements indicate that bacterial adaptation during infection is compartmentalized by tissue microenvironments and prior history, and establish HeteroTyper as a practical, generalizable route to quantify infection-relevant phenotypic diversity on solid media at routine, high throughput.

papers.title: Rhizobia transform legume nodules via native T-DNA transfer systems
papers.abstract: Agrobacteria can deliver transfer DNA (T-DNA) into plant cells, causing tumorous growth. This process, agrobacteria-mediated transformation (AMT), underlies plant genetic engineering and has been regarded as an evolutionary innovation specific to these pathogens. By screening 63,759 alphaproteobacterial genomes for T-DNA border sequences, we identify mini-T-DNAs in diverse rhizobial genera. Each typically encodes a single cargo, a RolB/RolC family protein or a distant rhizobial homologue. We show that native rhizobia-mediated transformation (RMT) systems deliver these mini-T-DNAs into the root nodules of common bean, pea, and chickpea, where the cargo genes are expressed, with no signal in adjacent root tissue. RMT systems share VirG-dependent activation of the core virulence regulon but respond to distinct upstream signals. Our genome screen identifies many additional candidate T-DNA transfer systems, and phylogenetic analysis places their genes into two of the many type IV secretion system (T4SS) clades. RMT systems occur in both clades, together with other systems unrelated to T-DNA transfer, and typically have an ancestral-like T4SS configuration. In contrast, AMT systems occupy a single subclade, consistent with later acquisition of their T4SS module. AMT and RMT thus represent two specialized outcomes of an older, more widespread capability for bacteria-to-plant DNA transfer.

papers.title: The chromatin-associated PWO proteins interface with circadian and epigenetic signaling to regulate flowering time in Arabidopsis
papers.abstract: Flowering time is a major determinant of reproductive success in plants and is regulated by several interconnected pathways which converge on few key flowering time-related genes. In the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana (Arabidopsis), both the circadian clock and chromatin-associated proteins integrate environmental cues to coordinate flowering (Staiger et al. 2013; Nohales and Kay, 2016; Du et al. 2019; Haider and Farrona, 2024). However, how the circadian-epigenetic signaling crosstalk regulates this crucial developmental transition has still been underexplored. PWWP-DOMAIN INTERACTORS OF POLYCOMBS 1 and 2 (PWO1 and PWO2) are chromatin-associated proteins that have been linked to the regulation of histone 2A (H2A) mono-ubiquitination (ub) (H2Aub) levels (Zheng et al. 2023). PWO1 and PWO2 also affect flowering time (Hohenstatt et al. 2018; Khan et al. 2026), but the underlying molecular mechanisms, their effects on clock genes, as well as their distinct contributions to flowering-time regulation remain mostly unknown.

papers.title: Neural Crest-Derived Endocardial Cells Required for Heart Valve Development
papers.abstract: Abnormalities in cardiac valves, which maintain unidirectional blood flow through the heart, affect 2-3% of people worldwide and are the most common form of structural heart disease (1).Yet the cell types that make up the valve, and how they communicate to direct development and homeostasis, remain poorly understood. Here, we identify a rare, essential population of highly secretory valve endocardial cells in mouse and human that derive from migrating neural crest cells. Ablation of these cells in mice caused perinatal lethality with thickened leaflets, stenosis, and regurgitation, mirroring human valve disease. This subset of endocardial cells uniquely expresses the secreted signaling protein parathyroid hormone-like hormone (Pthlh). Global disruption of Pthlh caused valve stenosis and lethality and neural crest-specific deletion produced similar valve disease, with impaired maturation of valvular interstitial cells and disrupted bone morphogenetic protein signaling. These findings identify a previously unrecognized cell type and signaling pathway essential for valve morphogenesis, with implications for the pathogenesis and treatment of human valve defects.
